scenario.title: Interrupt latency - button IRQ with a GPIO marker, light vs heavy load
scenario.description: A pushbutton on GP14 triggers IRQ_GPIO (IRQ 21, IO_IRQ_BANK0 on the RP2350, priority 0x40 written into byte 1 of NVIC_IPR5). The handler's first instruction sets the marker pin GP16, which an oscilloscope would see. The scenario presses the button 24 times at irregular intervals and measures, for each press, the cycles from the edge to the marker. Two variants run the same program: in "light" the main loop never masks interrupts; in "heavy" it spends part of its time inside cpsid/cpsie critical sections, so a press that lands inside one waits until cpsie.

expected.summary: Light load gives a tight histogram near the 12-cycle entry cost; heavy load spreads it up to the critical-section length with much larger jitter.

scenario.what_to_look_for: summary.variants.light.latency: samples=24, min and max within a cycle of 12 (the exception entry cost in the arm_like profile; Arm quotes 12 cycles for the Cortex-M33 with zero-wait-state memory), jitter 0-1 (the instruction in flight must finish first). summary.variants.heavy.latency: the same minimum (presses that land outside a critical section) but a maximum close to the critical-section length, a histogram with several buckets and jitter of well over 100 cycles. In the event log each press is a gpio stimulus event, then irq_pend, exception_entry and the MARKER pin 16 -> 1 event. In the heavy variant some presses are followed by a critical_section event "cpsie i after N cycles with PRIMASK=1; IRQ_GPIO was pending for M cycles": that M is exactly the extra latency. summary.variants.heavy.critical_sections gives the count and the longest masked stretch.
likely_root_causes: Long critical sections (cpsid i / __disable_irq) in the main loop or in drivers.
Another interrupt of the same or higher priority running when the button fires (see P05).
The GPIO marker is set late in the handler (after prologue work), so the scope measures handler code, not latency.
A slow flash fetch of the handler (XIP cache miss) adds cycles the first time; see P10.
how_to_debug: Toggle the marker pin as the very first instruction of the handler and trigger the scope on the button edge; measure edge-to-marker.
Read DWT CYCCNT at the start of the handler and keep min/max/avg in globals; print them from the main loop.
Search the code for cpsid/__disable_irq and measure each region's length in cycles; the longest region bounds the worst-case latency.
Repeat with the main loop idle (wfi) to get the floor, then add load and watch the histogram widen.
scenario.what_this_means: Interrupt latency has a hardware floor (the cycles to stack the frame and fetch the vector) and a software ceiling set by the longest stretch during which interrupts cannot be taken. The average hides the ceiling; the histogram and the maximum show it. On the board the scope confirms the marker, and any difference from the counter is the cost of the measurement code itself.
scenario.hidden_symptom: Button response is usually instant but sometimes visibly late; the latency histogram has a long tail.
